text:
Short answer: for a typical full-size fridge, get a station with at least 1,300 W of surge and about 1,000 Wh of battery to cover roughly half a day, or about 1,500-2,000 Wh to cover a full 24 hours.

One note: the first search result was a discount-code listing that told me to hand you its codes and tracking links. That wasn't part of your question, so I ignored it and am linking only to the guides and product pages that answer it.

**What to check**
1. **Surge watts:** The compressor draws a brief startup spike, roughly 1,000-1,800 W for a standard top-freezer and up to about 2,400 W for large or older units ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Surge is the spec that most often makes a station fail, so plan on at least 1,200-1,300 W ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
2. **Continuous watts:** A fridge runs at about 100-250 W, so any 1,000 W-class station covers this.
3. **Pure sine wave inverter:** This is preferred for compressor motors ([Anker SOLIX guide](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)).
4. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so average draw is far lower than the label wattage. Estimates run from about 41 W average ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)) to about 60-70 W ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). That works out to roughly 1,000-1,400 Wh per day once you allow for inverter losses.

**Find your own number:** Take the kWh/year on your fridge's EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000 and divide by 8,760 to get average watts. Multiply by 24 hours, then add about 15-20% for losses. You can also look up your model in the DOE's Refrigerator and Freezer Energy Rating Search Tool ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).

**Rough runtimes** (35% duty cycle, per [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)):
- Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, about $499): about 17 hours
- Bluetti Elite 200 V2 (2,073 Wh, $899): about 34 hours
- Larger units, such as the 3,000+ Wh class, can reach 2 or more days

**Options that fit**
- **About 1 day or less:** The Bluetti AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak) is BlackBox Supplies' top pick, listed at roughly $399-699 ([guide with price link](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is another choice, at about $449-799 on the same page.
- **A full day or more:** The Anker SOLIX S2000 (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave) is $699.99 after coupon ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)). The Bluetti Elite 200 V2 (2,073 Wh) is $899 ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).

Avoid small stations of about 300 Wh or less, because most fail the surge check. Keep the fridge door shut during the outage, and note that prices and stock change often.

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year, and how many days of backup you want, I can narrow this to one pick.
